target: AG1’s opening claim that AI is broadly beneficial because it improves convenience, health, accessibility, and workplace safety
objection: These benefits are not enough to offset major tradeoffs in practice; AI often brings economic displacement, privacy/surveillance risks, reduced critical thinking, racial bias, and unsafe overreliance, so it may be a net harm rather than a net good.

target: AG1’s economic claim that automating routine tasks mainly makes work easier and more productive
objection: Automation can also reduce job security, weaken workers’ bargaining power, and concentrate profits among a small number of firms that control the models and data, so it can harm the economic well-being of workers and businesses.

target: AG1’s claim that AI improves health and quality of life
objection: AI health tools often require sensitive personal data, creating serious privacy and surveillance risks; if data is mishandled, people can face identity theft, discrimination, or tracking.

target: AG1’s claim that AI supports accessibility for people with disabilities
objection: Accessibility is not a blanket win because AI can misrecognize speech, give incorrect guidance, fail in edge cases, and create dependency on corporate platforms rather than genuine empowerment.

target: AG1’s claim that AI improves workplace safety
objection: AI safety systems can miss hazards and create false confidence, leading employers to reduce human oversight; safety based on opaque systems is therefore not truly robust.

target: AG1’s implicit claim that AI is acceptable if used responsibly and that critical thinking concerns are overstated
objection: When students and adults outsource explanation, drafting, and reasoning to AI, they practice less judgment and problem-solving, which erodes independent critical thinking.

target: AG1’s claim that AI benefits marginalized groups rather than harming them
objection: AI systems can reproduce and amplify racist patterns from training data and feedback loops, causing discriminatory outcomes in hiring, policing, lending, healthcare, and visibility online.

target: AG2’s assumption that the harms AG2 lists are inherent and unavoidable features of AI
objection: Many of the harms are implementation failures, not inevitable properties of AI, and can be addressed through design, governance, and responsible deployment rather than rejecting AI wholesale.

target: AG2’s claim that automation is a reason to reject AI because of job loss and weakened worker power
objection: Automation risk does not justify broad rejection; with retraining, wage support, and incentives for productive uses, AI can reduce drudgery, raise productivity, and shift demand toward higher-skill work.

target: AG2’s claim that AI necessarily creates privacy and surveillance harms
objection: AI systems can be designed with data minimization, consent, auditing, privacy-preserving techniques, and on-device processing, so privacy risk is not inevitable.

target: AG2’s claim that AI is bad for accessibility because assistive tools can fail
objection: Errors are not unique to AI; with testing, fallback options, and human support, AI can expand communication and independence for people with disabilities.

target: AG2’s claim that AI workplace safety is unreliable because it can miss hazards
objection: Safety tools can be built to require human confirmation, use clear thresholds, and log decisions, making AI a helpful aid to hazard detection and response rather than a source of unsafe overconfidence.

target: AG2’s claim that AI undermines critical thinking by default
objection: AI can also support critical thinking by coaching step by step, asking Socratic questions, generating practice problems, and forcing students to justify answers, so the effect depends on how it is used in education.

target: AG2’s bias argument that AI necessarily reproduces and amplifies discrimination
objection: Bias is real but not destiny; it can be measured across groups, mitigated through better data and modeling, and constrained through audits and accountability standards.

target: AG1’s claim that oversight can solve AI harms through audits, privacy controls, and bias testing
objection: Governance is not realistically enforceable at scale because model details are proprietary, deployment moves faster than regulators, and vendors can market “responsible use” without actually delivering it.

target: AG1’s assumption that firms will adopt privacy protections and human oversight when asked
objection: Profit incentives push companies toward data collection and labor-saving automation, so safeguards like data minimization and human-in-the-loop review are likely to be weakened when they conflict with revenue.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving design solves surveillance risk
objection: Even with on-device or privacy-preserving processing, AI systems still often collect identifiers, logs, and behavioral signals, and users cannot meaningfully consent to complex data practices they do not understand.

target: AG1’s claim that bias can be managed through audits and accountability
objection: Bias does not disappear; it can reappear under distribution shifts and feedback loops, so audits reduce some harms but do not guarantee fairness.

target: AG1’s claim that human-in-the-loop design makes AI safer
objection: Humans tend to trust fluent automation and rubber-stamp its outputs, so human involvement can create complacency rather than genuine safety.

target: AG1’s claim that high-risk AI can be controlled through phased, measurable deployment and enforceable gates
objection: Risk classification is contestable and companies benefit from ambiguity; they can label systems as merely “assistive” while those systems still shape major decisions, undermining the gatekeeping premise.

target: AG1’s claim that rollback and continuous monitoring can address AI harms
objection: Rollback cannot undo downstream damage that already happened, such as harmful hiring, lending, or guidance decisions that affected real people before the problem was detected.

target: AG1’s claim that monitoring can be done without worsening privacy risk
objection: Continuous monitoring usually requires additional behavioral and telemetry data, which recreates the very surveillance problem it is supposed to solve.

target: AG1’s claim that liability and procurement rules can counter profit incentives
objection: Liability is hard to enforce because victims must prove causation and access proprietary evidence, so accountability lags behind the speed of deployment.

target: AG1’s claim that calibrated adoption is better than broad opposition because AI benefits outweigh the risks
objection: The harms are structural and arise from the way AI is deployed at scale, so the problem is not isolated bad actors but the system itself; that makes broad restriction more appropriate than incremental governance.

target: AG2’s claim that governance proposals are unrealistic because they presume enforceability and transparency that do not exist
objection: Imperfect governance is not a reason for blanket rejection; systems can be deployed with enforceable obligations, verified performance evidence, and third-party evaluation under confidentiality.

target: AG2’s claim that because risks are systemic, AI should be broadly opposed
objection: Systemic harms call for systemic regulation of high-impact uses, not blanket opposition that also blocks accessibility, health support, and safety benefits.

target: AG2’s claim that continuous monitoring necessarily creates more privacy harm
objection: Monitoring can be done with privacy-preserving techniques such as aggregated metrics, synthetic or benchmark testing, and secure computation, so monitoring and surveillance are not the same thing.

target: AG2’s claim that contestability and redress cannot meaningfully address downstream harm
objection: High-stakes workflows can require human review, clear explanations, and appeal mechanisms, which reduce irreversibility and make harmful decisions contestable.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving monitoring avoids surveillance
objection: Even if framed as privacy-preserving, monitoring still requires data, tests, metrics, and sometimes sensitive datasets or proxy signals, so the privacy risk is not removed—only hidden in less-visible infrastructure.

target: AG1’s claim that contestability and redress can restore fairness after harm
objection: In practice users often are not told AI was used, explanations are opaque, and appeals are costly and information-asymmetric, so accountability mechanisms are often ineffective.

target: AG1’s claim that broad restriction would unjustly harm accessibility and safety
objection: Accessibility does not require high-capability general AI; narrower non-generative tools and human-supported services can meet many disability needs, so restricting general AI does not necessarily remove accommodations.

target: AG2’s claim that content-only scanning and limited-retention monitoring still amount to harmful surveillance
objection: Content-in-the-flow checks with short retention, minimal metadata, and strict access controls can mitigate risk more like spam filtering than persistent behavioral tracking, so monitoring does not inherently equal surveillance.

target: AG2’s claim that graduated interventions necessarily create unacceptable side effects
objection: Instead of immediate censorship, systems can use warnings, credibility scoring, provenance indicators, and ranking/routing changes, combined with transparent criteria and rapid appeal, to reduce harm without heavy-handed suppression.

target: AG2’s claim that accessibility can be handled without high-capability AI
objection: Many accessibility gains increasingly depend on advanced AI capabilities such as better speech recognition, adaptive navigation, real-time tutoring, and multimodal assistance, so broad restriction risks stalling those improvements.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving methods and user-centered guardrails can make AI safe
objection: Even privacy-preserving systems require building and tuning on large amounts of user-like data, which shifts rather than removes privacy risk; and probabilistic friction or labeling can still suppress minority communities through false positives.

target: AG1’s claim that high/low-risk gating can control general-purpose AI
objection: General-purpose AI can be rapidly repurposed, so systems labeled low-risk can quickly become high-impact tools, making category-based gating unstable in real deployment.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving techniques solve the data problem
objection: Independent evaluation still depends on vendor-controlled access to data, logs, and behavior, so the safeguards are not truly independent and remain vulnerable to proprietary opacity.

target: AG1’s claim that capability licensing can control misuse
objection: Once models are widely reachable, they can be fine-tuned, distilled, and redistributed, so licensing turns into an arms race of enforcement and circumvention.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can be used in education without harming critical thinking
objection: Even with scaffolding, users still outsource writing, reasoning, and decisions to AI, which can erode judgment and critical thinking over time.

target: AG1’s claim that compliance disclosures and third-party audits can make proprietary AI accountable
objection: Vendor-controlled audits and confidential disclosures keep key evidence and decision logic out of reach for affected people, so accountability exists more for regulators than for the public.

target: AG1’s claim that restricting high-stakes deployment is enough to control risk
objection: AI diffuses into ordinary apps, browsers, and productivity tools, blurring the line between high-stakes and low-stakes uses and making deployment-based controls hard to enforce.

target: AG1’s claim that education and workplace rules can prevent harmful outsourcing to AI
objection: Rules cannot fully overcome the convenience and incentive to use AI as a substitute for effort, so users will still delegate reasoning and writing in ways that erode independent thinking.

target: AG1’s broader conclusion that AI can be made good for society through calibrated governance
objection: AI’s harms are driven by market power, dependence, diffusion into everyday tools, and opaque vendor control, so risk-based governance and partial safeguards cannot reliably neutralize the structural harms in real-world conditions.
